subject: science
name: Tissues in Action
summary: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together for one job. Plants have growing (meristematic) and mature (permanent) tissues, including the transport tissues xylem and phloem; animals have epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue. Muscles and bones work together as the musculoskeletal system, and the totipotency of plant cells lets us grow whole plants by tissue culture.

topics.title: What is a tissue? Levels of organisation
topics.summary: A tissue is a group of similar cells with a common origin that together do a specific job; tissues build organs, and organs build organ systems.
topics.simple: In a big organism, cells don't all do everything. Similar cells group together to do one job — such a group is called a **tissue**. Tissues join to make organs (like the heart or a leaf), and organs work together as organ systems.
topics.explain:
A **tissue** is a group of cells that are similar in structure, usually have a common origin, and work together to perform a particular function.

**Levels of organisation:**
**cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism**
- Cell: a muscle cell
- Tissue: cardiac muscle tissue
- Organ: the heart (made of muscle, connective, nervous and epithelial tissues)
- Organ system: the circulatory system

**Division of labour:** in multicellular organisms, different groups of cells specialise in different jobs — some carry oxygen, some send messages, some contract. Each group becomes very good at its own task, and the whole body works more efficiently. A single-celled organism like *Amoeba* has to do everything inside one cell.

**Why plant and animal tissues differ:**
- Plants stay in one place, so they need a lot of **supporting** tissue, much of which is **dead** (it gives strength without needing food or energy).
- Plants grow throughout their life, but only in certain regions, which contain **dividing (meristematic) tissue**.
- Animals move around looking for food and mates, so they use more energy and most of their tissues are **living**.
- In animals, growth is more uniform across the body, so there is no separate 'growing tissue' at fixed places.
topics.example: A cricket team works like division of labour: bowlers, batters and the wicketkeeper each specialise, and the team does better than eleven people all trying to do everything.
keyPoints: Tissue = group of similar cells doing a specific job
Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
Division of labour makes multicellular organisms efficient
Plants: lots of dead supporting tissue; growth only in certain regions
Animals: mostly living tissues because they move and use more energy
keywords: why plant and animal tissues differ

topics.title: Meristematic tissue: where plants grow
topics.summary: Meristematic tissue is made of actively dividing cells; apical meristem increases length, lateral meristem (cambium) increases girth, and intercalary meristem adds length at the base of leaves and internodes.
topics.simple: Plants grow only at special places that have cells which keep dividing. These cells form **meristematic tissue**. The tips of roots and shoots make the plant longer, while a ring of dividing cells inside the stem makes it thicker.
topics.explain:
**Meristematic tissue** is made of cells that can keep dividing.

**Features of meristematic cells:**
- Actively dividing
- Thin cellulose walls
- Dense cytoplasm and a large, prominent nucleus
- Little or no vacuole (they don't need to store much)
- Packed closely with no spaces between cells

**Types, based on where they are found:**
1. **Apical meristem** — at the growing tips of stems and roots. Increases the **length** of the plant.
2. **Lateral meristem (cambium)** — along the sides of stems and roots. Increases the **girth** (thickness). This is why tree trunks get wider every year.
3. **Intercalary meristem** — at the base of leaves or at the internodes (the parts of the stem between nodes). Adds length in the middle of the plant. Grasses and bamboo grow this way, which is why lawn grass grows back after mowing.

**Differentiation:** new cells made by meristems gradually lose the ability to divide and take on a fixed shape and job. They become **permanent tissue**.
topics.example: When you cut the tip off a growing money plant stem, it stops getting longer at that point, because the apical meristem has been removed; side branches may sprout instead.
keyPoints: Meristematic cells divide actively
Thin walls, dense cytoplasm, big nucleus, no or tiny vacuoles
Apical → length (root and shoot tips)
Lateral (cambium) → girth
Intercalary → at base of leaves / internodes (grasses)
Differentiation turns meristem cells into permanent tissue

topics.title: Permanent plant tissues: simple and complex
topics.summary: Simple permanent tissues are epidermis, parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma; complex tissues are xylem (water and minerals up) and phloem (food both ways). Together they form the dermal, ground and vascular tissue systems.
topics.simple: Once plant cells stop dividing they become **permanent tissue**. Some are simple (one kind of cell): the skin (**epidermis**), soft filler (**parenchyma**), flexible support (**collenchyma**) and hard, dead support (**sclerenchyma**). Others are complex (several kinds of cells): **xylem** carries water up, and **phloem** carries food around.
topics.explain:
**Simple permanent tissues** (one type of cell):
- **Epidermis:** the outermost layer, usually one cell thick. It protects the plant. On leaves it often has a waxy **cuticle** that reduces water loss, and small pores called **stomata** (each surrounded by two guard cells) for gas exchange and transpiration.
- **Parenchyma:** living cells with thin walls, loosely packed with spaces between them. Stores food and fills up the plant. When it contains chloroplasts it can photosynthesise; in water plants it has big air spaces that help them float.
- **Collenchyma:** living, elongated cells whose walls are thickened at the corners with **pectin** (and cellulose). Gives **flexibility and mechanical support**, so leaf stalks and young stems bend without breaking.
- **Sclerenchyma:** **dead** cells with very thick walls stiffened with **lignin**, often with almost no space inside. Makes plant parts **hard and stiff** — e.g. the **husk of coconut**, the hard shells of nuts and fibres such as jute.

**Complex permanent tissues** (more than one type of cell) — the conducting or vascular tissues:
- **Xylem:** made of **tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres**. Most of these are **dead** (only xylem parenchyma is living). Carries **water and minerals upward** from roots to leaves.
- **Phloem:** made of **sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres**. All are **living except the fibres**. Carries **food** (made in leaves) **in both directions** — up and down — to wherever it is needed.

**Tissue systems:** plant tissues are organised into three systems — the **dermal** system (epidermis, protection), the **ground** system (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma — storage, photosynthesis, support) and the **vascular** system (xylem and phloem — transport).
topics.deep: Tracheids and vessels are long tubes; vessels are joined end to end like a pipeline. Because they are dead and hollow, water can move through them easily. Sieve tubes have perforated end walls called sieve plates, and the companion cells beside them help keep them working.
topics.example: The stringy fibres you pull off a celery or drumstick stalk and the hard husk of a coconut are made of strong-walled supporting cells, while the soft white part of a potato is mostly parenchyma storing starch.
keyPoints: Epidermis: protective outer layer; cuticle and stomata
Parenchyma: living, thin-walled, stores food
Collenchyma: living, pectin-thickened corners, flexibility
Sclerenchyma: dead, lignin, hardness (coconut husk)
Xylem: tracheids, vessels, parenchyma, fibres; mostly dead; water and minerals UP
Phloem: sieve tubes, companion cells, parenchyma, fibres; living except fibres; food BOTH ways
Tissue systems: dermal, ground, vascular

topics.title: Animal tissues: epithelial and connective
topics.summary: Epithelial tissue covers and lines body surfaces (squamous, stratified, columnar, ciliated, glandular); connective tissue binds and supports (blood, bone, cartilage, tendons, ligaments, areolar, adipose).
topics.simple: **Epithelial tissue** is the covering and lining of the body — like the skin and the lining of your mouth and intestines. **Connective tissue** holds things together and supports them — blood, bone, cartilage, tendons, ligaments and fat are all connective tissues.
topics.explain:
**Epithelial tissue** — the covering or lining tissue. Cells are packed tightly with almost no space between them, forming a continuous sheet that protects and controls what passes through.
- **Simple squamous:** a single layer of thin, flat cells. Lines blood vessels and the air sacs of the lungs, where substances must pass through easily.
- **Stratified squamous:** flat cells in **many layers**. Found in the skin's outer layer and the lining of the mouth, where there is wear and tear.
- **Columnar:** tall, pillar-like cells. Lines the inside of the intestine, where food is absorbed.
- **Ciliated:** columnar cells with hair-like **cilia** on top. Found in the windpipe; the cilia beat to push mucus and dust out.
- **Sensory:** specialised cells that pick up stimuli, e.g. in the nose and tongue.
- **Glandular:** epithelial cells folded inwards to form glands that **secrete** substances, e.g. sweat glands.

**Connective tissue** — cells are spread out in a **matrix** (a jelly, liquid or hard material between the cells). It joins, supports and fills.
- **Blood:** a fluid connective tissue. The liquid **plasma** carries red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets, and transports gases, food, hormones and wastes.
- **Bone:** hard and strong; its matrix contains calcium and phosphorus compounds. Forms the skeleton.
- **Cartilage:** firm but flexible; smooths joint surfaces and shapes the nose and ear.
- **Tendons:** strong, tough cords that **join muscle to bone**.
- **Ligaments:** elastic bands that **join bone to bone** at joints.
- **Areolar tissue:** found between the skin and muscles and around organs; fills space and helps repair.
- **Adipose tissue:** stores **fat**, found below the skin and around organs; acts as insulation and an energy store.
topics.example: When you sprain your ankle, the ligaments joining the bones there are stretched or torn. The bendy tip of your nose and the flap of your outer ear are cartilage.
keyPoints: Epithelium: tightly packed covering and lining
Simple squamous: blood vessels, lung air sacs; stratified squamous: skin, mouth
Columnar: intestine (absorption); ciliated: windpipe
Glandular epithelium forms glands
Connective tissue: cells in a matrix
Tendon = muscle to bone; ligament = bone to bone
Blood is fluid connective tissue; adipose stores fat

topics.title: Animal tissues: muscle and nervous
topics.summary: Muscle tissue contracts: skeletal (voluntary, striated, multinucleate), smooth (involuntary, spindle-shaped) and cardiac (branched, striated, involuntary, tireless). Nervous tissue is made of neurons with a cell body, dendrites and an axon.
topics.simple: **Muscles** move the body by contracting (getting shorter). Some you control (arm muscles), some work by themselves (stomach, heart). **Nervous tissue** carries messages as electrical signals through special cells called **neurons**.
topics.explain:
**Muscle tissue** is made of long cells called **muscle fibres** that contain special proteins which let them **contract** and relax.

1. **Skeletal (striated) muscle**
- Attached to bones; moves the body
- **Voluntary** — works when we decide
- Cells are long, cylindrical, unbranched and **multinucleate** (many nuclei)
- Show light and dark bands called **striations**

2. **Smooth (unstriated) muscle**
- Found in the walls of the stomach, intestine, blood vessels, and in the iris of the eye
- **Involuntary** — works without our control
- Cells are **spindle-shaped** (pointed at both ends) with one nucleus and no striations

3. **Cardiac muscle**
- Found only in the **heart**
- **Involuntary** and **striated**
- Cells are **branched**, cylindrical, usually with one nucleus
- Contracts and relaxes rhythmically all through life and **does not get tired (fatigue)**

**Nervous tissue** is found in the brain, spinal cord and nerves. Its cells, **neurons**, receive stimuli and carry messages very quickly.
A neuron has:
- a **cell body** containing the nucleus and cytoplasm
- **dendrites** — short, branched extensions that receive messages
- an **axon** — a single long extension that carries the message away from the cell body
Some neurons in our body are extremely long, among the longest cells we have. Many neurons bundled together make a **nerve**.
topics.example: Picking up a pen uses skeletal muscle (you decide). Food being pushed along your intestine uses smooth muscle (automatic). Your heartbeat is cardiac muscle, working every second without rest.
keyPoints: Skeletal: voluntary, striated, multinucleate, attached to bones
Smooth: involuntary, spindle-shaped, unstriated (stomach, intestine, blood vessels)
Cardiac: involuntary, striated, branched, never tires
Neuron = cell body + dendrites + axon
Dendrites bring signals in; axon carries them away
Nerves are bundles of neurons

topics.title: Tissues in action: the musculoskeletal system
topics.summary: Bones, muscles, tendons, ligaments and cartilage work together to support and move the body; muscles work in antagonistic pairs (biceps and triceps) around joints such as ball and socket, hinge, pivot and fixed joints.
topics.simple: Muscles can only **pull**, never push. So they work in pairs: one pulls a bone one way and its partner pulls it back. Bones meet at **joints**, and different joints allow different movements — the shoulder swings all round, the elbow bends like a door hinge, the neck turns, and the skull bones don't move at all.
topics.explain:
The **musculoskeletal system** is a great example of many tissues working together: bone and cartilage (support), skeletal muscle (movement), tendons (muscle to bone), ligaments (bone to bone) and nerves (control).

**Antagonistic muscle pairs:** a muscle can only **contract (pull)**; it cannot push. So muscles work in pairs with opposite effects.
- To **bend** the arm at the elbow, the **biceps** (front of upper arm) contracts and the **triceps** relaxes.
- To **straighten** the arm, the **triceps** (back of upper arm) contracts and the biceps relaxes.

**Joints** — where two or more bones meet:
- **Ball and socket joint:** a rounded end of one bone fits in a cup of another, allowing movement in all directions. Examples: **shoulder, hip**.
- **Hinge joint:** movement back and forth in one direction only, like a door. Examples: **elbow, knee**.
- **Pivot joint:** one bone rotates on another. Example: the joint in the **neck** that lets the head turn.
- **Fixed (immovable) joint:** bones are locked together and do not move. Example: the bones of the **skull**.

**Protective parts of the skeleton:**
- **Skull** — a hard case protecting the brain
- **Vertebral column (backbone)** — a chain of small bones (vertebrae) that supports the body and protects the spinal cord, while still letting us bend
- **Rib cage** — **12 pairs of ribs** that protect the heart and lungs, and move during breathing
topics.example: Do a slow bicep curl with a water bottle: feel the front of your upper arm harden as it lifts. Now straighten your arm against a wall — the back of your arm (triceps) tightens instead.
keyPoints: Muscles only pull; they work in antagonistic pairs
Biceps bends the elbow; triceps straightens it
Ball and socket: shoulder, hip (all directions)
Hinge: elbow, knee (one direction)
Pivot: neck (rotation); fixed: skull (no movement)
Skull protects brain; backbone protects spinal cord; 12 pairs of ribs protect heart and lungs

topics.title: Totipotency and plant tissue culture
topics.summary: Totipotency is the ability of a single plant cell to form a whole plant; in tissue culture, cells dedifferentiate into a callus, which then redifferentiates into shoots and roots.
topics.simple: Amazingly, one living plant cell holds all the instructions to rebuild the whole plant. This power is called **totipotency**. Scientists grow tiny pieces of a plant on a special jelly with food and hormones: the cells first form a shapeless lump (**callus**), which then grows shoots and roots and becomes a new plant.
topics.explain:
**Totipotency:** a single plant cell can divide and develop into a complete plant. The idea was proposed by **Gottlieb Haberlandt** (1902).

**Plant tissue culture** uses totipotency to grow new plants from small pieces of plant tissue in the laboratory.

**Steps:**
1. A small piece of plant tissue (an **explant**, e.g. from a shoot tip or leaf) is taken and sterilised.
2. It is placed on a sterile **nutrient medium** (a jelly containing sugar, minerals, vitamins and plant hormones).
3. **Dedifferentiation:** the specialised cells lose their special features and start dividing again, forming an unorganised mass of cells called a **callus**.
4. **Redifferentiation:** by changing the hormones, the callus is made to form shoots and roots, giving small **plantlets**.
5. The plantlets are moved to pots and slowly hardened before planting in the field.

**Uses:**
- Producing **thousands of identical plants** quickly from a small amount of tissue
- Getting **disease-free** plants
- Saving **rare and endangered** plants
- Growing plants in any season
topics.example: Many banana, orchid and sugarcane saplings sold to Indian farmers are raised by tissue culture, so every plant is identical to a high-yield, healthy parent.
keyPoints: Totipotency = one plant cell can form a whole plant (Haberlandt, 1902)
Explant → nutrient medium with hormones
Dedifferentiation → callus (unorganised mass)
Redifferentiation → shoots and roots → plantlets
Uses: many identical, disease-free plants; saving rare species

keyConcepts.meaning: A group of similar cells, usually of common origin, working together to perform a specific function.
Different groups of cells in a multicellular organism specialising in different jobs, which makes the body more efficient.
Plant tissue made of actively dividing cells; found at root and shoot tips (apical), in the cambium (lateral) and at the base of leaves or internodes (intercalary).
Living plant tissue with cell walls thickened at the corners by pectin; gives flexibility.
Dead plant tissue with thick, lignin-hardened walls; gives hardness and strength (e.g. coconut husk).
Complex plant tissue of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and fibres that carries water and minerals upward; mostly dead cells.
Complex plant tissue of sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and fibres that carries food in both directions; living except fibres.
Animal tissue of tightly packed cells that covers and lines body surfaces and organs.
Animal tissue whose cells lie in a matrix; it binds, supports and fills (blood, bone, cartilage, tendons, ligaments, areolar, adipose).
A tendon joins muscle to bone; a ligament joins bone to bone.
A nerve cell, with a cell body, dendrites that receive signals and an axon that carries signals away.
A pair of muscles with opposite actions, such as the biceps (bends the elbow) and triceps (straightens it).
The ability of a single plant cell to develop into a complete plant.
An unorganised mass of dividing cells formed by dedifferentiation in plant tissue culture.

commonMistakes: Mixing up tendons and ligaments — a tendon joins muscle to bone; a ligament joins bone to bone.
Saying xylem carries food — xylem carries water and minerals upward; phloem carries food in both directions.
Thinking all phloem cells are dead — only phloem fibres are dead; in xylem, most cells are dead except xylem parenchyma.
Confusing collenchyma (living, pectin, flexible) with sclerenchyma (dead, lignin, hard).
Writing that cardiac muscle is voluntary because it is striated — it is striated but involuntary.
Saying muscles can push — muscles only pull, which is why they work in antagonistic pairs.
Calling the knee a ball and socket joint — the knee and elbow are hinge joints; the shoulder and hip are ball and socket.
revision: Tissue = group of similar cells doing one job; cell → tissue → organ → organ system.
Plants: lots of dead supporting tissue and growth only at meristems; animals: mostly living tissue.
Apical meristem → length; lateral (cambium) → girth; intercalary → base of leaves/internodes.
Parenchyma stores food; collenchyma (pectin) gives flexibility; sclerenchyma (lignin, dead) gives hardness.
Xylem: tracheids, vessels, parenchyma, fibres — water and minerals up, mostly dead.
Phloem: sieve tubes, companion cells, parenchyma, fibres — food both ways, living except fibres.
Four animal tissues: epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous.
Simple squamous lines blood vessels and lung air sacs; stratified squamous forms skin; ciliated lines the windpipe.
Tendon: muscle to bone. Ligament: bone to bone. Blood is a fluid connective tissue.
Skeletal: voluntary, striated, multinucleate. Smooth: involuntary, spindle. Cardiac: involuntary, striated, branched, tireless.
Biceps bends and triceps straightens the elbow (antagonistic pair).
Ball and socket: shoulder, hip; hinge: elbow, knee; pivot: neck; fixed: skull. 12 pairs of ribs.
Tissue culture: explant → dedifferentiation → callus → redifferentiation → plantlets.

faqs.q: What is the difference between xylem and phloem?
faqs.a: **Xylem** carries **water and minerals** from the roots **upward**; most of its cells (tracheids, vessels, fibres) are **dead**. **Phloem** carries **food** made in the leaves **in both directions**; its cells (sieve tubes, companion cells, parenchyma) are **living**, except the phloem fibres.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a tendon and a ligament?
faqs.a: A **tendon** joins a **muscle to a bone** — it is tough and not very stretchy, so the pull of the muscle moves the bone. A **ligament** joins a **bone to another bone** at a joint and is somewhat elastic.

faqs.q: Why are plant and animal tissues different?
faqs.a: Plants stay in one place, so they need a lot of strong supporting tissue, much of it dead, and they grow only at certain regions (meristems). Animals move about for food and safety, use more energy, and so most of their tissues are living; their growth is more uniform through the body.
keywords: why plant and animal tissues differ

faqs.q: How is cardiac muscle different from skeletal and smooth muscle?
faqs.a: Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart. Like skeletal muscle it is **striated**, but like smooth muscle it is **involuntary**. Its cells are **branched**, and it contracts rhythmically throughout life **without getting tired**.

faqs.q: What is callus in tissue culture?
faqs.a: A **callus** is a shapeless mass of dividing cells. It forms when cells from a plant piece placed on a nutrient medium lose their specialisation (**dedifferentiation**). With the right hormones, the callus later forms shoots and roots (**redifferentiation**) to give new plantlets.

quiz.q: Which meristem increases the girth (thickness) of a stem?
quiz.explain: The lateral meristem, or cambium, adds width; apical meristem adds length.

quiz.q: The husk of a coconut is made mainly of:
quiz.explain: Sclerenchyma has dead cells with thick, lignin-hardened walls, making the husk hard and fibrous.

quiz.q: Which plant tissue gives flexibility to leaf stalks, thanks to cell walls thickened with pectin at the corners?
quiz.explain: Collenchyma is living tissue with pectin-thickened corners, allowing bending without breaking.

quiz.q: Which statement about phloem is correct?
options: It is made of tracheids and vessels
It carries food in both directions
quiz.explain: Phloem carries food up and down; its cells are living except the fibres. Tracheids and vessels belong to xylem.
Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone.

quiz.q: The inner lining of the windpipe, which sweeps mucus and dust upward, is made of:
quiz.explain: Ciliated epithelium has hair-like cilia that beat to move mucus out of the airway.

quiz.q: Which muscle is striated, involuntary and made of branched cells?
quiz.explain: Cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle but involuntary, with branched cells, and it never tires.

quiz.q: In a neuron, the long extension that carries messages away from the cell body is the:
quiz.explain: The axon carries signals away; dendrites receive signals.

quiz.q: When you bend your arm at the elbow:
options: The triceps contracts and biceps relaxes
Both contract at the same time
The biceps contracts and triceps relaxes
quiz.explain: The biceps pulls the forearm up; its antagonist, the triceps, relaxes. The reverse straightens the arm.

quiz.q: Which pair are both hinge joints?
quiz.explain: The elbow and knee move in one direction like a door hinge; shoulder and hip are ball and socket joints.

quiz.q: In plant tissue culture, the unorganised mass of cells formed after dedifferentiation is called:
quiz.explain: Dedifferentiated cells form a callus, which later redifferentiates into shoots and roots.

quiz.q: Why do plants have a large amount of dead supporting tissue while animals mostly have living tissue?
options: Plants have no cells that can divide
Plants are stationary and need strength without spending energy, while animals move and need more living, active tissue
Animals do not need any support
Dead tissue helps plants move towards light
quiz.explain: Stationary plants benefit from strong dead tissue that needs no upkeep; animals move and use more energy, so most tissues are living.
